name: Serpstat
subcategory: keyword research, backlinks and rank tracking
tagline: Track selected keywords and import competitor research into a local project

tiers.name: Individual
tiers.limits: 5 projects; 100 searches/day; 10,000 position checks; 30,000 audit pages; 50,000 export rows; 1 user.

tiers.name: Team
tiers.limits: Unlimited projects; 500 searches/day; 150,000 audit pages; 250,000 export rows; 3 users.

tiers.name: Team x2
tiers.limits: 1,000 searches/day; 100,000 position checks; 300,000 audit pages; 500,000 export rows; 6 users; 400,000 API credits.
tiers.notes: Exact monthly price was not reliably exposed.

tiers.name: Agency
tiers.limits: 5,000 searches/day; 500,000 position checks; 1,500,000 audit pages; 2,500,000 export rows; 30 users.

pricing.freeTierCaps: no free tier (7-day trial on Individual and Team only)
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual (annual saves up to 27%); trials require a refundable $1 card verification and auto-renew unless cancelled
pricing.hiddenCosts: Team limits can be expanded through paid customization; public unit prices vary by selected capacity.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Serpstat, track selected keywords and import competitor research into a local project. The hard boundary is proprietary search, backlink, advertising, and competitor datasets, plus proprietary web index and data acquisition.
coreLoopDIY: Track a user-supplied keyword set, import competitor research into a local project, collect permitted search-result snapshots at low volume, and show trends without pretending to recreate a commercial web index.
requirements: approved search-data API or manual imports
whatYouLose: proprietary search, backlink, advertising, and competitor datasets
moatNotes: proprietary web index and data acquisition
ongoingBurden: proxy and API costs, crawl freshness, geolocation, anti-bot rules, keyword normalization, storage, and data QA
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Serpstat because customers pay for a continuously refreshed web-scale dataset whose collection cost dwarfs the dashboard around it. The recurring cost buys proxy and API costs, crawl freshness, geolocation, anti-bot rules, keyword normalization, storage, and data QA, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: SerpBear
priorArt.desc: Open-source search ranking tracker for owned keyword sets.

alternatives.name: OpenSEO
alternatives.desc: Tracks keywords and stores competitor domain research locally; DataForSEO supplies the facts and charges by the spoonful.

rejectedAlternatives.name: SerpBear
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Excellent at tracking your keywords, entirely uninterested in importing competitor research.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Serposcope
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Rank tracking only, archived in 2024 and last touched in January 2022.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Individual plan and a small owned-keyword tracker DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Serpstat in an empty repository.
Use Python 3.12, FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Playwright, and a small React frontend; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: track a user-supplied keyword set, import competitor research into a local project, collect permitted search-result snapshots at low volume, and show trends without pretending to recreate a commercial web index.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create projects with domains, keywords, target country, language, device, and tags.
Fetch rankings only through the configured compliant API and enforce a daily budget.
Store raw result snapshots and normalized positions so every chart is auditable.
Display current rank, movement, best rank, URL changes, and a compact SERP history.
Import backlink and keyword files from third-party tools without claiming independent coverage.
Add scheduled runs, failure alerts, CSV export, retention settings, and database backups.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out building a general web crawler or backlink index.
Deliberately leave out circumventing search-engine access controls.
Deliberately leave out traffic estimates presented as observed first-party data.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
